title: February 2026 Spotify for Developers update: thread
text:
Hey everyone, I’ve created this thread to provide an open space for discussion, feedback, concerns or ideas on an upcoming update to Spotify for Developers access. We’ve shared a blog post that explains what’s changing and why. Please use this thread to share any thoughts about the update. We'll try our best to answer questions but we're not in a position to respond to every reply in this thread. Where appropriate we will add updates in this post to ensure visibility to all commentators (instead of burying the information in the comments). I am not able to reply to individual DM’s but please note that everything shared here will be read and considered. If related questions or discussions pop up elsewhere in the community, we’ll link or merge them back here so everything stays in one place. Thanks for taking the time to share your thoughts. Update: After some review and following feedback we have received from you below, we have decided to postpone endpoint access changes for existing Development Mode integrations. All other changes, including the Spotify Premium requirement, the authorized user cap and one Client ID per developer limit, will take effect for existing Development Mode integrations as planned. Newly created Development Mode Client IDs remain subject to the updated rules introduced on February 11. We will share additional details on revised timelines as they become available. You can find the full details in the blog post , and we’ll add links to any supporting documentation there as it becomes available.

All other changes, including the Spotify Premium requirement, the authorized user cap and one Client ID per developer limit, will take effect for existing Development Mode integrations as planned. Newly created Development Mode Client IDs remain subject to the updated rules introduced on February 11. We will share additional details on revised timelines as they become available.
It's ultimately Spotify's discretion as to which APIs remain available and the access/quotas applied thereto, but this is a really disappointing update. It seems to be the final nail in a coffin already saturated with nails. The quota updates last year (limiting developers to an allowlist of 25 users that can use the app unless they are a company with 250k users and other extremely high-bar requirements) has already materially killed off the ability for people to build applications using Spotify's platform. This more recent update (limiting access even further from 25 → 5 users) and removing some key endpoints like listing a user's playlists ) is poor for developers and the users of their apps, but it is merely one more step down the road of killing the developer platform. As I said, if Spotify wants to go in this direction then that's a business choice, but it would be great if this could be discussed candidly rather than speciously, as though the developer platform at Spotify still exists and serves developers, that innovation with Spotify's APIs is encouraged and supported. Presumably this is in response to abuse of APIs and data mining Spotify's catalogue by some bad actors (though this is just a guess); it's disappointing that an esteemed engineering company such as Spotify's attempt to solve that problem is to pull developer access from their platform rather than actually fixing the root problem. No shade to you, @ThePodFather, as the messenger, but as a developer that just built a web app that helps me  (and ideally my friends) organise my Spotify library in a fun way, it's just galling and disappointing to see things getting even worse. edit: in my original post I mentioned that the API endpoint for fetching a user's playlists was being removed; this isn't the case – you can still fetch playlists of the current user (aka `me`) but not of other users, which is still an annoying limitation, but not as bad as I thought.

title: 403 on /v1/playlists/{id}/items for 198 of 471 own/followed playlists, plus   POST /tracks returns
text:
Plan Premium Country USA Device API Operating System MacOS My Question or Issue Building a single-user personal data tool against the Web API. Authorization Code Flow, app in Development Mode, my own account is on the app's User Management allowlist. Reads mostly work; hitting three distinct failures I can't explain from the docs. App / account - Spotify user: 1225751719 - Auth: OAuth Authorization Code Flow - Scopes granted (confirmed in the /api/token response): user-top-read user-follow-read user-read-recently-played user-library-read user-read-playback-state user-read-currently-playing user-read-playback-position playlist-read-private playlist-read-collaborative playlist-modify-private playlist-modify-public Issue 1 — GET /v1/playlists/{id}/items returns 403 on 198 of my 471 playlists Same access token, same code path. 273 succeed (200 with full contents). 198 fail (403 {"error":{"status":403,"message":"Forbidden"}}). Breakdown of the 198: - 150 are owned by me directly - 48 are owned by other users (friends, distributors, etc.) - GET /v1/playlists/{id} (metadata) returns 200 for the same playlists. Only the /items subpath is blocked. No clean rule predicts which playlists fail. The failing set spans the entire timeline — by year-in-title alone it includes 2011, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2025, 2026. ~120 of the failures are undated personal playlists ("Isbell Primer", "To Share", monthly archives, etc.). Sample failing playlist I own: GET /v1/playlists/2DZTTP1Zfom5omcUsjgv7B/items?limit=1 Authorization: Bearer <access_token> → 403 {"error":{"status":403,"message":"Forbidden"}} Sample succeeding playlist I own: GET /v1/playlists/5pNKJFPKCiYr9AwhSJq1ai/items?limit=1 Authorization: Bearer <access_token> → 200 OK Both owned by me, both private, both authorized by the same token in the same session. What differentiates them? Issue 2 — POST /v1/users/{me}/playlists returns 403 with no detail POST /v1/users/1225751719/playlists Authorization: Bearer <access_token> Content-Type: application/json {"name": "test", "public": false, "collaborative": false} → 403 {"error":{"status":403,"message":"Forbidden"}} No Retry-After, no error detail. Scopes include both playlist-modify-private and playlist-modify-public. Issue 3 — POST /v1/playlists/{id}/tracks returns 429 with Retry-After: 68591 (~19 hours) Manually created an empty playlist in the Spotify app, then attempted to add a single track via API: POST /v1/playlists/1mScFPQlLKCCzKpOqjGEjn/tracks Authorization: Bearer <access_token> Content-Type: application/json {"uris": ["spotify:track:46TalNUrIxhDeHHJDDMzzn"]} → 429 Too many requests Retry-After: 68591 Body: "Too many requests" 68591 seconds = ~19 hours. No successful write activity from this app prior. This reads as a near-zero daily write quota in Development Mode, not ordinary rate limiting. Issue 2's 403 (no Retry-After) and Issue 3's 429 (with Retry-After) appear to be the same underlying quota expressed differently by different endpoints. --- Questions 1. Are read 403s on /items for user-owned playlists a known restriction for apps registered after November 2024? Is there a property of the playlist (snapshot age, track licensing state, something else) that determines access? 2. Is the write quota for Development Mode apps effectively zero in the current configuration? If so, where is that documented? 3. Is Extended Quota Mode the only path to functional playlist write operations for personal-use apps, even at the scale of one user creating one playlist? Happy to share the app's client ID privately or attach a HAR if useful.
Hey @Verysecur3 Thanks for posting in the Spotify Community! I notice you try to mix of getting tracks with items and posting tracks with tracks . To clarify, you should use items for every type of item, with POST and GET request. This change was announced in this Migration Guide . This works only for playlists you made (except generated ones) and playlists you are a collaborator on. This change was announced in this blog post . For information about rate limits, I will refer you to this page . I hope this helps. If you need anything else, feel free to ask! title: [Feature Proposal] Expose folders in the api
text:
I have a app that allows creating playlists. It would be really great if I could put all the playlist that my app makes into a certain folder so it is in its own nice category. I propose the api endpoints for folders to  be: [GET] me/folders?limit=...&offset=... Returns playlist ids of playlists in the folder folder name creation date folder id [PUT] me/folders?name="...." You could have playlists_ids in the  body for batch moving playlists to the folder like {"playlist_ids": ["....", "...''], "name":"...."} But you could also just reuse the update playlist details endpoint [DELETE] me/folders?id="..." Should probably not delete the playlists in the folder You could just use the already existing modify playlist details endpoint to move playlists into a folder like so: [PUT] /playlists/{playlist_id} Body: {"folder_id":"..."} It would also be great that when you create a playlist you could specify a folder id. This is nice because it saves a request if you want to put the playlist in the folder anyway. [POST] /user/{user_id}/playlist Body: {"folder_id": "...." } I think the folder endpoints could just fall under the user-library-modify scope It would be great if this were to be added to the api as it would lead to a lot of new creative uses for the api and managing playlists. People could program their apps to put the playlists that their app creates into separate folders. I think uses would really appreciate this as their library stays much more organized.
I would really like to see this feature as well. It has come up as a problem / request multiple times over the years but never gains any traction.
Sad that I have to bring this post back from the dead after more than a year, but this is by far the best proposal I've seen for the Spotify API. This is a feature that is incredibly needed, and it's clearly already in the user data since folders sync between desktop and iOS. I heavily use folders and it's frustrating when I can't find one of my 300 playlists on any web app or even official (although soon to be e-waste) hardware like the Car Thing. I wish there was more support for this.

title: Restore Web API write access for individual developers (Development mode) —   follow/playlist endpoi
text:

Since the recent changes, ALL write endpoints (PUT /me/following, playlist modify) return 403 Forbidden for my own account in Development mode — even with the correct scopes (user-follow-modify) and a freshly created app. Read endpoints (GET) work fine and return 200 with the same token/scopes. title: B2B Enterprise Catalog Audit Platform — Appropriate Path for Web API Extended Access?
text: Hello Spotify Developer Community, My name is Raul Rodriguez, and I am contacting you on behalf of Creation Music LLC / Creation Music Group, a registered music administration, catalog audit, publishing administration, and rights-management company based in Florida. We are developing iCatalogIQ, a B2B catalog intelligence, rights-verification, and catalog-protection platform for professional music companies, labels, publishers, catalog owners, attorneys, rights administrators, and enterprise music teams. iCatalogIQ is not designed as a consumer-facing Spotify companion app measured primarily by mass monthly active users. Instead, the platform is intended to support professional and enterprise catalog-audit workflows for rights holders and organizations that manage large volumes of music assets. A key purpose of iCatalogIQ is to identify catalog theft, unauthorized duplication, duplicate releases, metadata manipulation, ownership inconsistencies, and rights conflicts by comparing DSP-facing catalog information against verified internal records, publishing data, distribution data, royalty records, ISRC information, songwriter/publisher records, and other rights-management sources. In the music industry, unauthorized duplications and incorrect catalog entries can cause serious harm. They can redirect royalties, create ownership confusion, interfere with proper royalty accounting, dilute official catalog performance, create false metadata trails, and make it difficult for rights holders to identify who is collecting revenue from their works. iCatalogIQ is being built to help rights holders detect these problems earlier and generate structured audit evidence that can support correction, escalation, or rights-administration action. Our platform helps review and verify artist discographies, albums, singles, track metadata, release dates, identifiers, duplicate versions, conflicting releases, unauthorized uploads, and mismatches between public DSP catalog data and the underlying rights records maintained by labels, publishers, distributors, administrators, and catalog owners. We are preparing iCatalogIQ for enterprise licensing conversations with major music catalog owners and industry partners. These organizations manage large catalogs, so our expected Spotify Web API usage would be driven by authorized catalog-review workflows and catalog-protection activity, not casual consumer activity. Because of this, we would like to confirm whether Spotify has an appropriate review path for B2B enterprise rights-administration and catalog-audit platforms that may not fit the standard consumer-app MAU model. Our use case is not based on having hundreds of thousands of consumer users logging into Spotify through our app. It is based on professional catalog analysis for rights holders, labels, publishers, and catalog administrators who need scalable metadata verification across large catalogs. iCatalogIQ uses Spotify data only for legitimate catalog identification, metadata comparison, rights verification, catalog protection, duplicate detection, and audit-support workflows. The platform does not use Spotify data to train machine learning models, create an unauthorized replica of Spotify, redistribute Spotify content, bypass Spotify functionality, or replace the Spotify user experience. iCatalogIQ has already implemented caching and rate-conscious request handling to reduce repeated Spotify Web API calls and avoid unnecessary requests for the same catalog data. The platform is designed to reuse previously retrieved metadata where appropriate, control refresh frequency, and support compliant retry/backoff behavior when Spotify returns HTTP 429 or Retry-After responses. Could someone please advise whether we should proceed through the standard Partner Application / Extended Quota request, or whether there is a more appropriate process for this type of B2B enterprise catalog-audit, catalog-protection, and rights-verification use case? title: Authorisation in a CLI app
text:
I'm trying to write a Python CLI program (no associated webpage, entirely on-device, mostly for my own personal use) that will create a playlist. This means I have to use authorisation code flow, not client credentials. However, all of the authorisation docs seem to assume you'll have some sort of webpage to redirect to after authorisation, which my program does not (being a CLI-only program with no online presence). How would I get the authorisation code in these circumstances? Solved! Go to Solution.
I've normally tackled this by creating manual one-time authorization logic. If the application hasn't been authorized yet, I spin up a process to listen on a local port (ex: http://127.0.0.1:8080 ) and have it extract the code and state from the resulting query string. I then verify the state and exchange the code for an access token and refresh token. The refresh token, client ID, and client secret then get saved somewhere so authorization does not need to be performed again. I'm primarily a .NET dev, so I'm not as familiar with Python specifics, but it looks like spotipy might already have this built in ( https://spotipy.readthedocs.io/en/2.26.0/ ). Hey there @albanderv , Thanks for posting here in the Community and welcome. We hope you don't mind us moving your post as it fits better here in a thread. In order for you to stop watching videos on the Now Playing View on the desktop app, you need to click the Switch to audio button to go back to the audio view. By closing the Now Playing View in the desktop app, you'll also stop watching videos. Now, if perhaps you're seeing an 8-second visual loop that shows instead of the album art, that'd be the Canvas . It appears in the Now Playing View instead of the album artwork. You can disable this feature by first clicking on your profile picture and then going to Settings . Once there, locate Display and under that, toggle the option Display short, looping visuals on tracks (Canvas) off. title: "Can't play this content, Exclusive mode is on"
text:
Every time I try to play a song, I get a pop-up saying "Can't play this content. Exclusive mode is on, so this content won't play. Turn it off in settings to keep listening" but when I check in the settings, exclusive mode isn't enabled. I've tried switching to a different audio input that also doesn't have it enabled, and it still won't work. Is this happening to anyone else?
Make sure that your playback device is set to 44.1 kHz sampling frequency (16 or 24 bit). Set this in Windows sound settings. If in windows setting you don't have the 44.1 kHz option, check any device-specific control panel or app. My PreSonus interface comes with the 'Universal Control" app, and Windows only sees the sampling frequency that was set there. When I had it on 48 kHz, I could not use Exclusive mode. Switched to 44.1, all good. I imagine it is possible that some Spotify content may be encoded a different sampling frequency than 44.1, and then the device setting would have to be changed to match. Annoying, but the point of the exclusive mode is that it guarantees no resampling, so that's the price one has to pay.

The workaround is to disable it by following these steps: In the Nvidia Shield’s settings , go to: settings > device preferences > display & sound > advanced sound settings and disable "Match content audio resolution - Preserve audio bit depth and sampling rate over HDMI" . After this is done, either a force stop of the Spotify app is recommended and/or a cold restart of the device by unplugging the power cord (and other cables as well should be helpful).
